performers: Vladimir de Pachmann, piano (his own Baldwin)
intro: Pachmann recorded the Nocturne in D♭ major, Op. 27 No. 2, on his own Baldwin piano at Hayes in June 1925. The critic who reviewed the disc that December praised its phrasing and noted that the famous pianist stayed silent between the notes.

sections.label: A · Melody over D♭ accompaniment
sections.mNote: The left hand plays alone before the melody enters on F.

sections.label: B · Duet in thirds
sections.mNote: B♭ in the bass changes the harmony to minor

sections.label: C · Opening melody again, D♭ major
sections.mNote: The melody restarts on F above D♭, marked dolce.

sections.label: D · Duet in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: G♯ in the bass under close right-hand voices

sections.label: E · Third statement of the theme, D♭
sections.mNote: The opening theme returns before a long ornamental passage.

sections.label: F · Coda over D♭ pedal
sections.mNote: Changing chords above a recurring D♭ bass

cues.title: Opening bars, left hand
cues.text: For one bar the left hand plays alone, spreading D♭ major into groups of six semiquavers. The melody then begins on F. Chopin marks it Lento sostenuto, a slow, sustained song above an unbroken accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 1–4, Lento sostenuto and dolce. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Melody in thirds, bars 10–13
cues.text: The right hand doubles the melody in thirds as the bass moves to B♭. The new phrase is marked espressivo, and both voices share its short rests and ornaments.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Review in The Gramophone, 1925
cues.text: The critic signing K.K. in The Gramophone, December 1925, welcomed this record with relief: “he does not utter a word the whole time”. He praised the playing (“What a fine builder he is!”) and complained about the recorded piano.
cues.evidence: K.K., review of HMV DB 860, The Gramophone, December 1925, pp. 338–339. https://archive.org/stream/gramophone-1925-12/Gramophone%201925-12_djvu.txt

cues.title: Recording session, Hayes, 1925
cues.text: Pachmann brought his own Baldwin to the Hayes session on 26 June 1925. The new electrical process recorded the piano clearly enough for the reviewer in The Gramophone in December to note that some notes sounded splendid and others clanged. The critic nevertheless praised the pianist’s spirit.
cues.evidence: Session date, place, piano and electrical process: https://archive.org/details/hmv-db860-chopin-nocturne-no8-op27no2-etudes-op25no3-waltz-no7-op64no2. Contemporary comments: The Gramophone, December 1925, pp. 338–339, https://archive.org/stream/gramophone-1925-12/Gramophone%201925-12_djvu.txt

cues.title: Third statement of the opening melody
cues.text: A falling run brings back the low D♭ and the opening melody. The right hand begins its third statement on the same F. The melody then turns into a long run of small notes.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Pedal on D♭, bars 62–68
cues.text: The bass holds D♭. Above it the chords change while the right hand descends in pairs of notes, marked dolcissimo, and the left hand continues its semiquavers across the keyboard.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Rising sixths and final chord
cues.text: The right hand rises in sixths, marked dolcissimo e diminuendo (very sweetly and growing softer). The final D♭-major chord is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 75–77: rising sixths, dolcissimo e diminuendo, pianissimo and final fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
